articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran Designation Update
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced an update to its Iran designations on November 9, 2026. This action is part of the ongoing effort to address Iran's destabilizing activities.

Further details regarding the specific entities or individuals designated, and the implications of these designations, are expected to be clarified through associated guidance or press releases from the Treasury Department.
These updates underscore the U.S. government's continued pressure on Iran through economic sanctions, targeting various sectors and actors deemed to be supporting illicit activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related Designations
body: On November 6, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) implemented new Iran-related designations. These actions aim to further restrict financial and material support for the Iranian government and its associated entities.

The designations are part of a broader strategy to counter Iran's nuclear program, support for terrorism, and human rights abuses. Specific details of the designated parties were not immediately released but are anticipated to follow.
These measures reinforce the existing comprehensive sanctions regime against Iran, which prohibits most transactions involving U.S. persons without specific authorization.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber and Criminal Organizations, Issues Cuba-Related Determination
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 5, 2026, targeting cyber-related and transnational criminal organizations. Concurrently, OFAC issued new designations and a determination related to Cuba.
The Cuba-related actions follow previous measures in May 2026 that allowed for sanctions against foreign companies and banks supporting the Cuban government under Executive Order 14404.
These designations aim to disrupt illicit financial networks and further pressure the Cuban government, aligning with the long-standing U.S. embargo against Cuba.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Updates Listings, and Amends Venezuela GL
body: On November 4, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and updates to existing Iran-related listings. This action was accompanied by the publication of an Iran-related OFAC Alert.

Additionally, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question. This indicates a continued focus on both the Iranian and Venezuelan sanctions programs, with adjustments to facilitate certain transactions while maintaining overall pressure.

The amendments to Venezuela-related general licenses have been a feature of the program since January 2026, offering broad licenses for the oil, gas, and mining sectors, though transactions outside these terms still require specific licenses.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026. This amendment modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran.
General Licenses are often issued to permit specific activities that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions programs, aiming to mitigate unintended humanitarian or economic impacts.
The details of this amended license will be crucial for entities engaged in permitted activities with Iran, as it may alter the scope or conditions of previously authorized transactions.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo Entities
body: On October 28, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting entities related to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
These actions are part of ongoing efforts to counter proliferation financing from North Korea and address human rights abuses and corruption in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The designations aim to disrupt financial networks supporting these activities and reinforce international sanctions regimes against both nations.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking and Rejecting Transactions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on October 26, 2026, regarding blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC.

These amendments provide updated guidance for financial institutions and other entities on their obligations under OFAC sanctions programs, particularly concerning the handling of blocked property and rejected transactions.
The revised FAQs aim to clarify compliance requirements and assist in the accurate reporting of sanctions-related activities to OFAC.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations, and Issues New General Licenses
body: On October 21, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations. Concurrently, OFAC removed certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea.

In addition to these actions, OFAC issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended Frequently Asked Questions. This indicates a dynamic approach to sanctions, with both new restrictions and targeted relief.

The removal of designations for Belarus and North Korea suggests a recalibration of sanctions against specific entities or individuals, while the new general licenses aim to facilitate certain transactions under the Iran and Russia programs.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements PAIPA Designations and Issues Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026. These designations are aimed at safeguarding American intellectual property from theft and illicit acquisition.
Alongside the designations, OFAC issued associated General Licenses to provide clarity and authorization for certain activities that might otherwise be impacted by these new measures.
These actions highlight the U.S. government's commitment to protecting intellectual property rights and deterring malicious actors who seek to exploit American innovation.

Details of the specific violations were outlined in the settlement agreement, which typically involve transactions with sanctioned entities or in sanctioned jurisdictions.
This penalty highlights the importance of robust compliance programs for companies operating internationally to avoid inadvertent breaches of sanctions regulations.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Pays $11,662,930 in OFAC Settlement
body: Bank of America, N.A. has settled with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for $11,662,930. This settlement addresses 475 apparent violations of multiple sanctions programs, including those related to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

The violations, occurring between September 18, 2021, and April 24, 2025, involved approximately $14.83 million in transactions. These included payments through blocked banks, flaws in alert prioritization, delays in watchlist updates, and mishandling of accounts.

This OFAC penalty is part of a larger, coordinated enforcement action by the U.S. Treasury Department, which also saw FinCEN assess a $1.2 billion penalty and the OCC impose a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America for widespread anti-money laundering and sanctions compliance failures.

articles.headline: ECB Poised for Final Rate Hike in December Amid Persistent Inflation Risks
body: The European Central Bank (ECB) is widely expected to implement a final deposit rate hike in December, according to a recent Reuters poll of economists. This move would push the deposit rate to 2.75%, surpassing the ECB's estimated neutral range.

Despite this anticipated 'final' hike, over a third of economists foresee an additional increase in early 2027. This outlook is driven by persistent inflation, which remains double the ECB's 2% target, and ongoing risks from elevated energy costs and low natural gas storage levels ahead of winter.

ECB Chief Economist Philip Lane has warned that underlying inflation could rise even if headline inflation falls, emphasizing the Governing Council's commitment to stabilizing inflation at its target in the medium term. Markets are currently pricing in two to three hikes by the end of next year, reflecting the uncertainty surrounding inflation and potential energy shocks.

articles.headline: OCC Announces October 2026 Enforcement Actions, Including Penalties for BSA/AML Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released its enforcement actions for October 2026, highlighting several significant measures against financial institutions and individuals. Among these, American Express National Bank in Sandy, Utah, received a Cease and Desist Order and a $350 million civil money penalty for deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance program, including failures in timely suspicious activity report (SAR) filings and customer due diligence.

Bank of America, National Association, based in Charlotte, North Carolina, was also assessed a $750 million civil money penalty for similar BSA compliance program deficiencies, including failures to timely file SARs and sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information. This penalty is part of a larger, coordinated action by the U.S. Treasury Department, which also involved FinCEN and OFAC.

Additionally, the OCC issued Orders of Prohibition against Jennifer Hamblin, a Vault Teller at Fifth Third Bank, N.A., for embezzling approximately $292,000, and Christopher Organista, a Former Operations Processor at U.S. Bank National Association, for embezzling approximately $194,131 in customer funds. These actions underscore the OCC's commitment to deterring violations and reinforcing individual accountability within the banking sector.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: BIS Extends Suspension of 'Affiliates Rule' for Entity List Enforcement Until January 2027
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has extended the suspension of its 'Affiliates Rule' until January 10, 2027. This rule, originally issued in September 2025, would extend Entity List, Military End-User List, and certain sanctions-based licensing requirements to foreign entities owned 50% or more by listed parties.

The suspension, which was set to expire on November 9, 2026, was initially implemented as part of the U.S.-China 'Busan Agreement' trade truce in October 2025. The extension aligns with the broader trade truce, which Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced in September would also be extended through January 10, 2027.

While the rule remains suspended rather than withdrawn, companies are advised to continue preparing ownership-based screening and due diligence procedures in anticipation of its potential reinstatement in January 2027. The Affiliates Rule aims to close loopholes that have allowed subsidiaries not explicitly named on the Entity List to acquire controlled U.S. items without a license, even if owned by a listed parent.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
